newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss hit back at D'Amato's Holocaust charges.
newsitem.headline: Swiss hit back at D'Amato's Holocaust charges.

text.p: Switzerland's diplomatic troubleshooter hit back at U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato on Friday, saying he was sensationalising isolated facts in his accusation that the Swiss profited from Nazi Germany's mass murder of Jews.

Thomas Borer, a senior diplomat, has been assigned to counter the bad publicity Switzerland is receiving over its handling of unclaimed assets after World War Two, which mostly belonged to Jews who perished in the Holocaust.
Going onto the offensive, he wrote to D'Amato, a leading campaigner on the issue, suggesting a meeting but rejecting the senator's claim that the Swiss were too biased to probe their own past.
A genuine historical review must analyse all the facts and documents available, he said.

"By contrast, publishing single documents out of context and without regard to the historical realities constitutes sensationalism and throws doubts upon the seriousness of purpose," Borer told D'Amato, chairman of the powerful Senate Banking Committee.
Switzerland was determined to uncover the truth and redress any wrongs from its financial dealings with Holocaust victims or Nazis, he wrote in a letter released by his ministry.
D'Amato has used declassified U.S. documents to allege Berne used the bank accounts of missing Polish Jews to pay off Swiss citizens for property seized by Communist Poland.
Berne has acknowledged it had a compensation accord with Poland after the war but is still probing whether money from the accounts actually went to Swiss citizens.

Borer wrote that Switzerland welcomed help in uncovering the truth. "However, such a dialogue presupposes mutual confidence and respect which, I regret to say, has sadly been missing on your side up to now."

The Swiss parliament is set to give final approval in December to a commission of historians empowered to lift banking secrecy in limited cases as they conduct a sweeping review of neutral Switzerland's wartime role as a financial centre.
A separate panel agreed by Jewish groups and Swiss bankers is also searching for dormant accounts of Holocaust victims.

Borer, who knows Washington from a 1993-1994 stint in the Swiss embassy there, took charge last week of a diplomatic task force created to toughen Berne's responses to a wave of criticism from world Jewish groups and D'Amato.

He told Reuters on Friday he had summoned Swiss ambassadors from the United States, Israel and most Western and Eastern European capitals to a strategy talk in Berne on November 15 on countering Holocaust accustions.
